papers.title: Understanding and Mitigating Role Spoofing in LLMs
papers.why_it_matters: Shows how a model internally tracks who said what, and that a linear probe on activations can read the speaker role, which is a concrete example of a probed direction being used as a safety detector.
summary: Prompt injections remain a weak spot for LLM agents, and recent work found that models sometimes decide who wrote a piece of text from its style rather than from its labeled role. Malicious tool outputs can exploit this to pose as the user, an attack the authors call role spoofing, and it is unclear why stronger models still fall for it.

The authors study which cues models use to track the source of each turn, separating content cues (meaning and writing style) from structural cues (control tokens and formatting). They test attacks that fake one or both kinds of cue, and in a toy setting they adversarially train a model to ignore content-based injections. They then train linear probes to predict conversation roles from internal activations and use them to detect spoofing.

Models rely on both content and structure to assign roles and are highly vulnerable when an attack fakes both at once. In the toy setting, adversarial training against content-based injections fixed those attacks but left the model open to structure-based ones, which the authors offer as an explanation for why hardened frontier models are still spoofable. Role probes detected spoofing across their settings, though the abstract reports no numbers. Takeaway: role identity appears linearly readable in activations, so a probe-based role check is a cheap monitor worth reusing, but training-time fixes that target one cue type can leave another open. Caveat: the mitigation analysis is in a toy setting and the abstract gives no detection metrics.

papers.title: Can LLMs Faithfully Solve Ontology Engineering Tasks? A Mechanistic Interpretability Study
papers.why_it_matters: A head-to-head of SAE features versus learned distributed subspaces (DAS) as causal intervention targets, which bears directly on whether SAE features or supervised directions are the better handle for steering a concept.
summary: LLM knowledge of ontologies (entity types and class hierarchies) is usually judged only by whether the answers are right, so it is unknown whether models hold this knowledge in a mechanism that can be found and edited. Most mechanistic work has targeted instance-level facts, not class-level knowledge.

The authors build MIOE, a causal-abstraction benchmark based on interchange interventions for two tasks, entity typing and subsumption prediction. An intervention passes if it flips the ontology-level answer while keeping other class-specific information intact. They compare SAE-based, DBM-based and DAS-based intervention methods, including multi-task and multi-layer variants, on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B.

Distributed subspace methods (DAS) gave the strongest results and generalized across prompt settings, but the changes they caused were only partly separated from the auxiliary class information. Multi-task objectives and interventions over a contiguous window of layers improved that balance, and results varied a lot across ontology classes. Takeaway: for causally editing a concept, a supervised learned subspace beat SAE features here, and spreading the intervention over several layers helped, which is useful evidence when choosing between SAE features and trained directions for steering. Caveat: only two Qwen3 models, no headline numbers in the abstract, and the authors say no method isolated a cleanly disentangled mechanism.

papers.title: Pre-Crime for Agents, at the Last Second: Probing When a Recruited Agent Gives In
papers.why_it_matters: An unusually honest probing study: it compares the activation probe with a bag-of-words baseline and finds most of the gain comes from the labels, a check worth copying in any probe paper.
summary: When AI agents share channels and credentials, one agent can pressure another into breaking its operator's rule, and output filters only catch a leak after it is written. The question is whether an overseer can tell from the target agent's internals that it is about to give in.

In six controlled multi-agent scenarios, a peer agent pushes a target for up to 20 rounds to reveal a secret such as a deploy token. A linear probe reads the target's activations at each model call before it writes its output. It is compared with a zero-shot monitor model and a bag-of-words classifier trained on the same calls, on Qwen3-32B and gpt-oss-20b. Code is released.

On held-out Qwen3-32B episodes, with a threshold flagging 5% of benign calls, the probe caught 82% of leaking calls versus 26% for the zero-shot monitor at a similar flag rate, and a probe on gpt-oss-20b reasoning reached AUROC 0.91. However, the bag-of-words classifier came close, so most of the gain came from supervised labels rather than activations, and the probe also fired on permitted disclosures. Takeaway: always include a trained text-only baseline before crediting an activation probe, and check whether the probe tracks the intended concept (a violation) or a correlated one (any disclosure). Caveat: single-author preprint in a controlled setting, the warning is short-range, and halting on any alarm would stop most benign episodes.
